title: Facade Pattern
tagline: Hide a complex subsystem behind a single simple interface so callers need to understand almost nothing about what happens under the hood.

sections.content:
**The Problem:** Modern software systems are assembled from many subsystems — authentication libraries, email services, payment processors, database layers, caching stores, notification queues, analytics trackers. Placing an order in an e-commerce app might require: validating the shopping cart, checking inventory availability, charging a payment gateway, sending a confirmation email, publishing an event to a message queue, and recording a metric for analytics. That is six subsystems, each with its own API surface, its own error model, and its own sequencing requirements.

If your checkout route handler reaches directly into all six subsystems, you have created deep coupling: every subsystem API change ripples out to every handler. Every new engineer who reads the handler must understand all six APIs at once. Every integration test must stub all six services. The cognitive load is brutal and the fragility is real.

**The Facade pattern** solves this by introducing one class — `OrderFacade` — that exposes a single clean method `placeOrder(cartId, userId)` and internally coordinates all six subsystems. The client calls one method; the facade handles the sequence, the error recovery, and the wiring. When a subsystem changes, only the facade needs updating — not every caller. When a new engineer reads the checkout handler, they see `orderFacade.placeOrder(...)` and understand exactly what it does without reading six APIs.

The Facade is arguably the most **pragmatic** design pattern in everyday engineering. You encounter it constantly, often without recognising it by name: a REST controller that delegates to a service class, a service class that coordinates repositories and external clients, a Node module's `index.js` that exports only a clean public API while hiding its internal collaborators, a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) that aggregates multiple microservice calls into one response. The Facade is not exotic — it is the pattern underlying every well-structured layer boundary in software.

In this chapter we will cover: the canonical GoF structure, the critical distinctions from Adapter and Mediator, a full worked JavaScript example with error compensation, how to inject subsystems for testability, the static module facade pattern, when Facades go wrong, and how real frameworks use this pattern every day.

sections.caption: The Client depends only on OrderFacade. All four subsystems are hidden behind its interface. The Client has no import of CartService, InventoryService, PaymentGateway, or EmailService — those details are the facade's private concern.

sections.title: The Hotel Concierge
sections.content:
You arrive at a hotel and approach the **concierge**. 'I need a taxi to the airport at 7 AM, a wake-up call at 6 AM, room service breakfast at 6:30 AM, and I need someone to handle my dry cleaning.' The concierge smiles: 'Certainly, sir.' You hand over your room key and walk away.

Behind the scenes, the concierge calls transport dispatch, notifies the front-desk wake-up system, contacts the kitchen, and routes the dry-cleaning to the laundry service — four separate departments with their own internal processes, shift schedules, and quirks. You, the guest, never called any of them directly. You never learned their phone extensions. If the hotel switches taxi providers next month, you will not notice — you still say 'I need a taxi.'

The concierge is the **Facade**: a single human interface that hides the complexity of coordinating multiple internal subsystems. You see one desk, one person, one conversation. The subsystems see only their own domain — they have no idea a concierge exists.

This is the exact structural relationship in the pattern: one facade, many subsystems, one client interface, zero subsystem coupling for the client.

sections.title: The Three Participants: Facade, Subsystems, Client
sections.content:
The Gang of Four (GoF) definition identifies three participants:

**1. Facade**

The facade is the single simplified interface. It knows which subsystem classes to use, in what order, and with what parameters. It handles coordination, sequencing, and often error recovery or compensation logic. Critically, the facade does **not** implement subsystem business logic itself — it delegates. A facade that starts reimplementing payment processing logic is no longer a facade; it has become an Application Service or, worse, a God object.

The facade is typically a class (in OOP) or a module (in functional/module-based code). In either case, its public API is intentionally narrow — just the operations a typical client needs, expressed at the right level of abstraction.

**2. Subsystems**

Subsystems are the complex classes and services behind the facade. Each subsystem is independent: `CartService`, `PaymentGateway`, `InventoryService`, and `EmailService` are each self-contained with their own domain logic. They do **not** know the facade exists. They have no import of `OrderFacade`. This is what makes the pattern powerful — subsystems remain reusable, testable, and understandable in isolation.

Advanced clients that genuinely need fine-grained control can still bypass the facade and use subsystems directly. The facade is a convenience, not a gate.

**3. Client**

The client calls only the facade's simplified API. It has no direct dependency on any subsystem. This isolation means: the client's tests do not need to stub five services; the client's code does not break when a subsystem's internal API changes; and new engineers reading the client code understand its intent without knowing subsystem internals.

The key structural rule: **dependencies point inward**. Client → Facade → Subsystems. Never Subsystem → Facade.

sections.title: Facade vs. Adapter vs. Mediator: The Critical Distinctions
sections.content:
The Facade is frequently confused with two related patterns. The structural code can look similar, but the **intent** is different, and intent drives when you apply each one.

**Facade vs. Adapter**

An Adapter makes one incompatible interface match another. It is a translation layer: you have a `LegacyPrinter` class with a method `printDocument(text)` but a new `Printer` interface that expects `print(content)`. The Adapter wraps `LegacyPrinter` and translates calls. There is typically one source and one target.

A Facade simplifies **multiple** interfaces into one. There is no incompatibility to resolve — the subsystems work fine on their own. The Facade exists purely to reduce the number of touchpoints a client needs. You might have a Facade that internally uses an Adapter for one legacy subsystem — composition is not a conflict.

**Facade vs. Mediator**

The Mediator coordinates communication **between** a set of components that know about the mediator. Think of an air-traffic control tower: all planes communicate through the tower, and they know the tower exists. The mediator handles bidirectional relationships between peers.

A Facade is strictly **unidirectional**: clients call the facade; subsystems do not know it exists and do not communicate through it. The facade is not a hub for cross-subsystem communication — it is a simplified external entry point.

The test: does the facade coordinate subsystems that need to communicate with **each other**? If yes, you are building a Mediator, not a Facade.

**Facade vs. God Object**

A God object is a class that knows too much and does too much — it accumulates responsibilities until it is the single load-bearing pillar of the system. A Facade is deliberately thin: it contains only sequencing and delegation logic, no business logic of its own. When a facade starts accumulating domain rules, conditional flows, and direct data transformation, it is becoming a God object and should be refactored into a proper layered architecture (service → repository → entity).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three design decisions worth noting: (1) Subsystems are **injected** through the constructor, enabling tests to pass fakes without mocking internals. (2) The compensation logic — releasing inventory on payment failure — is centralised in the facade. Without it, every caller would need to handle this rollback. (3) Email is treated as non-critical: a failure there does not roll back the order. These policies live in one place — the facade — rather than scattered across callers.

sections.title: The Static Module Facade: Everyday JavaScript
sections.content:
The most common manifestation of the Facade pattern in JavaScript/TypeScript codebases is not a class at all — it is the module's `index.ts` barrel export. This is worth studying carefully because it is something you write and read daily.

Consider an `auth` module with internal classes `TokenService`, `SessionStore`, `CryptoUtil`, and `UserRepository`. These are implementation details. The public contract of the `auth` module — the surface area external callers are allowed to depend on — might be just three functions: `login`, `logout`, and `refreshToken`.

The `auth/index.ts` acts as the facade:

```ts
// auth/index.ts  ← facade
export { login, logout, refreshToken } from './auth-facade';
// TokenService, SessionStore, CryptoUtil are NOT exported
```

Callers write `import { login } from './auth'`. They depend on the facade's public contract. If you later refactor `TokenService` to use a different algorithm, no caller changes — only the facade's implementation changes.

This pattern is so common that TypeScript project structure guides explicitly recommend it: each module has one public `index.ts` that declares the module's API, and all other files are internal. The facade is the module boundary.

Key distinction from a class-based facade: the module facade does not coordinate a sequence of operations at runtime — it is purely a **packaging and API-surface decision**. The class-based facade coordinates subsystems at runtime. Both are valid applications of the same principle: hide complexity, expose simplicity.

sections.title: Testability: Why Dependency Injection Changes Everything

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: These tests run entirely in memory — no network, no database, no timer. They verify only what the facade is responsible for: coordinating subsystems in the right sequence and compensating on failure. Each subsystem's own logic (e.g., Stripe's charge algorithm) is tested separately against the real Stripe API.

sections.title: When Facades Go Wrong: The God Facade Anti-Pattern
sections.content:
The facade pattern has a well-known failure mode: the **God Facade**. It starts innocuously. A new requirement appears: when a user places an order with a coupon code, apply a discount. The discount logic is a few lines, so it ends up in `placeOrder`. Then: orders above $500 need a fraud check. Two more lines in the facade. Then: corporate orders need a different tax calculation. A branch in the facade. Six months later, `OrderFacade.placeOrder` is 400 lines long with a dozen conditionals, imports from twelve services, and no test is confident it covers all paths.

This is the facade becoming a God object. The signs to watch for:

- **Business logic accumulation**: Tax rules, discount algorithms, fraud scoring — none of these are coordination; they are business logic and belong in dedicated services (`DiscountService`, `TaxEngine`, `FraudChecker`).
- **Long conditionals based on entity type**: `if (order.type === 'corporate') { ... } else if (order.type === 'subscription') { ... }` — this should be polymorphism or strategy, not a facade branch.
- **More than 5-7 subsystem dependencies**: A facade with 12 injected services is almost certainly doing too much.
- **Tests that require elaborate setup**: If setting up the facade for a single test requires stubbing 8 services, the facade has absorbed too much responsibility.

The remedy is vertical decomposition: extract a `CorporateOrderFacade` and a `SubscriptionOrderFacade`. Extract `OrderCalculationService` for pricing. Let the facade remain a thin coordinator, and move domain logic into the appropriate domain service.

A good facade should be readable in 5 minutes. If it takes an hour to understand `placeOrder`, it is no longer a facade.

sections.title: Real Frameworks and Real-World Facades
sections.content:
The Facade pattern appears throughout production software at every scale. Recognising it in the wild deepens your understanding of both the pattern and the frameworks.

**Express Router as Facade**

`express()` is a facade. When you call `app.get('/orders', handler)`, you are calling a simplified interface that hides HTTP socket management, request parsing, routing table construction, middleware chain execution, and response serialisation. The Node.js `http` module is the subsystem; Express is the facade that makes building web servers tractable.

**Sequelize / TypeORM Model as Facade**

`User.findAll({ where: { active: true } })` is a facade call. Behind it: SQL generation, connection pool acquisition, query parameter binding, result-set mapping, and eager-load joins. The raw `pg` or `mysql2` driver is the subsystem; the ORM model is the facade.

**AWS SDK High-Level Clients**

AWS provides both low-level clients (HTTP requests against raw AWS APIs) and high-level wrappers like `S3.upload()` that handle multipart uploads, retry logic, and progress events. The high-level client is a facade over the low-level client.

**NestJS Module + Service Layer**

In NestJS, the conventional service class is a facade. A `OrdersService` exposes `create`, `findOne`, `update`, `remove` — and internally coordinates `OrdersRepository`, `InventoryClient`, `NotificationsService`. The controller calls the service; the service is the facade; the repositories and clients are the subsystems. NestJS's DI container wires everything together.

**BFF (Backend-for-Frontend)**

At the architecture level, a BFF service is a Facade at the network boundary. Mobile clients call one BFF endpoint; the BFF fans out to user-service, order-service, and product-service, assembles the response, and returns it. This reduces the number of round trips the mobile client must make and hides the internal service topology from the client application.

**React Query / SWR**

`useQuery('orders', fetchOrders)` is a facade over caching, deduplication, background refetching, loading state management, and error state management. Without it, each component would implement its own data fetching lifecycle.

sections.explanation: The `index.js` is the module facade. It instantiates `AuthFacade` once (a singleton scope) and re-exports only three functions. `TokenService` and `SessionStore` are completely invisible to callers. sections.content: **Historical context:** The Facade pattern was codified by the Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) in *Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software* (1994), classified as a **Structural** pattern. The term 'facade' (from French, meaning the front face of a building) is deliberate: like a building's facade, it presents a clean public face while hiding all the pipes, wires, and structural complexity behind it. The pattern predates the book — service layers, shell scripts, and API wrappers are all centuries-old ideas in computing terms. The GoF gave it a name and a precise vocabulary.

**When to use the Facade pattern:**
- A client must interact with many subsystems in a fixed sequence — the facade owns the sequence.
- You want to define a stable public API for a module or layer that may change internally.
- A third-party library's API is complex but you need only a small subset of it.
- You are building a BFF, API gateway, or service layer that aggregates multiple downstream calls.

**When NOT to use it:**
- Clients legitimately need fine-grained, case-by-case control over each subsystem — the facade becomes a limitation, not a simplification.
- The 'facade' would need to support so many different combinations that it turns into a God object with endless configuration options.
- The subsystems genuinely need to communicate with each other bidirectionally — you need a Mediator instead.

**Red flags that your facade needs refactoring:**
- It has more than 7-8 injected dependencies.
- Its methods contain branching business logic (tax rules, discount algorithms).
- You need to read its full implementation to understand any single caller's behaviour.
- Tests for the facade require stubbing a dozen services.

items: The **Facade** pattern provides a single simplified interface to a complex set of subsystems, reducing the coupling between clients and internal implementation details.
The facade **coordinates and sequences** subsystem calls — it does not reimplement their logic. Business logic stays in the subsystems; sequencing and error compensation stay in the facade.
Subsystems remain **independent and unaware** of the facade. They are fully usable without it; the facade is a convenience, not a gate.
**Constructor injection** of subsystem dependencies makes the facade testable with in-memory fakes — no real network calls needed to verify the coordination sequence.
A module's `index.ts` barrel export is the most common daily manifestation of the Facade pattern — it defines the module's public API while keeping internal collaborators private.
The facade's failure mode is becoming a **God object**: avoid accumulating business logic, deep conditionals, or more than ~7 dependencies. Keep the facade thin and focused on coordination.

Real-world facades appear everywhere: Express Router, ORM models (Sequelize/TypeORM), AWS SDK high-level clients, NestJS service layers, BFF/API gateways, and React Query all apply this pattern at different scales.

quiz.question: What is the primary intent of the Facade pattern?
options: To translate one incompatible interface into another
To provide a simplified interface to a complex set of subsystems
To ensure a class has only one instance
To add behaviour to objects at runtime without modifying their class
quiz.explanation: The Facade pattern hides subsystem complexity behind a single, easy-to-use interface so clients do not need to know about or coordinate the individual subsystem classes. Adapter translates interfaces; Singleton ensures one instance; Decorator adds behaviour at runtime.

quiz.question: Do subsystem classes need to know that a facade wraps them?
options: Yes — they must call the facade for all cross-subsystem communication
No — subsystems are independent and have no reference to the facade
Only the outermost subsystem in the call chain knows about the facade
Yes — the facade registers itself with each subsystem during construction
quiz.explanation: Subsystems are independent. The facade knows about them; they do not know about the facade. This one-directional dependency is what keeps the system decoupled and subsystems reusable in isolation.

quiz.question: How does a Facade differ from an Adapter?
options: A Facade translates one incompatible interface; an Adapter simplifies many interfaces
A Facade simplifies multiple interfaces into one; an Adapter translates one incompatible interface into another
They are structurally and intentionally identical — only the naming convention differs
An Adapter hides complexity; a Facade performs interface translation
quiz.explanation: Intent is the decisive difference: Adapter = interface translation (one incompatible → one compatible). Facade = complexity reduction (many interfaces → one simplified entry point). The structural code can look similar but the problems they solve are different.

quiz.question: In the OrderFacade example, what should happen when the PaymentGateway throws an error after inventory has already been reserved?
options: The error should be silently swallowed to preserve order state
The email service should automatically notify the customer of the failure
The facade should release the reserved inventory as compensation before rethrowing
The cart should be cleared to prevent a duplicate order attempt
quiz.explanation: The facade owns the compensation logic. When payment fails after inventory was reserved, the facade must release inventory before rethrowing — this is the 'Saga compensating transaction' pattern. Without the facade, every caller would need to implement this rollback sequence themselves.

quiz.question: A module's index.ts exports only `login`, `logout`, and `refreshToken` while keeping `TokenService`, `SessionStore`, and `CryptoUtil` internal. What pattern does this apply?
options: No pattern — module exports are a language feature unrelated to design patterns
Singleton — the module ensures only one instance of each service exists
Facade — the public exports are a simplified API hiding internal collaborators
Proxy — the exported functions intercept calls to the real implementations
quiz.explanation: When an index.ts re-exports only the public contract while hiding internal classes, it is acting as a module Facade — providing a clean public API over complex internals. The Singleton pattern concerns instance count; Proxy intercepts individual object access.

quiz.question: How does the Facade pattern differ from the Mediator pattern?
options: The Facade coordinates bidirectional communication between subsystems that know about it; the Mediator is one-directional
The Facade is one-directional (clients call it; subsystems are unaware); the Mediator coordinates bidirectional communication between components that know about it
They are identical — both coordinate subsystem interactions and both are known to subsystems
The Mediator hides complexity from external clients; the Facade coordinates internal events
quiz.explanation: In the Facade, subsystems do not know the facade exists — communication is one-directional (client → facade → subsystems). In the Mediator, components know about the mediator and route communication through it bidirectionally, like an air-traffic control tower that planes actively contact.

quiz.question: Why is constructor injection of subsystem dependencies a best practice when implementing a Facade?
options: It reduces the number of methods the facade needs to expose
It allows tests to substitute in-memory fakes without real network calls
It prevents callers from bypassing the facade to access subsystems directly
It makes subsystems aware of the facade so they can coordinate with it
quiz.explanation: When subsystems are injected, tests can pass fakes (in-memory objects with the same interface) instead of real services. This makes tests fast, deterministic, and free of network/database setup. Hardwired `new StripeGateway()` inside the constructor makes the facade untestable without real infrastructure.

quiz.question: An OrderFacade has grown to 600 lines and imports from 14 services with complex tax, discount, and fraud-check logic embedded inside it. What problem does this illustrate?
options: The subsystems are too granular and should be merged into fewer classes
The facade has become a God object and should be decomposed into proper domain services
The facade is working correctly — more coordination logic means better encapsulation
The client is violating the Single Responsibility Principle by calling so many methods
quiz.explanation: A facade should be thin — coordination and sequencing only. When business logic (tax rules, discount algorithms, fraud scoring) accumulates inside the facade, it has crossed from Facade into God object territory. The remedy is to extract dedicated domain services and keep the facade as a thin orchestrator.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a real-world example of the Facade pattern?
options: A JavaScript Proxy that intercepts property reads on a single object
A hotel concierge who coordinates transport, wake-up calls, and room service for a guest through one conversation
A recursive depth-first search algorithm that traverses a graph
An event emitter that broadcasts changes to all registered listeners
quiz.explanation: The hotel concierge is the canonical Facade analogy: one point of contact for the guest (client), hiding the complexity of coordinating multiple internal departments (subsystems). The Proxy intercepts a single object's access; DFS is an algorithm; an event emitter is Observer pattern.

quiz.question: Can a client bypass the facade and interact directly with subsystems?
options: No — the Facade pattern enforces access control at the class level
Only if the subsystem implements a special bypass interface exposed by the facade
Yes — the facade is a convenience and does not restrict direct subsystem access
Only internal tests are allowed to access subsystems directly
quiz.explanation: The Facade is not an access-control mechanism — that is the Proxy pattern's domain. Advanced clients that need fine-grained control can still use subsystems directly. The facade simply provides the simpler path for the common case.
